These examples extend the basic univariate and bivariate workflow in
[Get started](example.html). Choose a topic below. Each article loads emhawkes
and defines its own model specifications and simulated data; the articles can
be run independently.

| Topic | Examples | Main features |
|:------|:---------|:--------------|
| [Multi-kernel models](multi-kernel-models.html) | Multi-kernel and synchronized intensity | Multiple decay scales, `type_col_map`, shared parameters |
| [Marked models](marked-models.html) | Linear impact | `impact`, `eta`, `rmark`, `dmark` |
| [State-dependent baseline](state-dependent-baseline.html) | Fosset spread and Hawkes/M/infinity queue | State from event counts, function-valued `mu` |
| [State-dependent impact](state-dependent-impact.html) | Hawkes flocking and bid-ask prices | State-dependent excitation, `lambda_component_n` |

The baseline examples are a useful starting point for state-dependent models.
The impact examples then introduce event-dependent shocks and adjustments to
accumulated intensity components.

## Multi-kernel models {#more-complex-models}

### Multi-kernel model

[Define and fit a model with multiple exponential kernels](multi-kernel-models.html#multi-kernel-model).
Use `type_col_map` to associate kernel columns with event types.

### Synchronized intensity model

[Share parameters across component functions](multi-kernel-models.html#synchronized-intensity-model).
This two-kernel model uses named parameters shared by `mu` and `beta`.

## Marked models {#extended-models}

### Linear impact model

[Add mark-dependent excitation and estimate the mark distribution](marked-models.html#linear-impact-model).
The examples cover a general `impact` function and the linear `eta` interface.

## State-dependent baseline

### Fosset's state-dependent spread model {#fosset-spread-model}

[Simulate and fit spread widening and narrowing](state-dependent-baseline.html#fosset-spread-model).
The narrowing baseline becomes zero at the minimum spread.

### A Hawkes/M/infinity queue: website visits and departures {#hawkes-infinite-server}

[Model visitor arrivals and departures](state-dependent-baseline.html#hawkes-infinite-server).
Hawkes arrivals increase the population, and each visitor has an exponential departure time.

## State-dependent impact

### Hawkes flocking model

[Make excitation depend on relative counting-process levels](state-dependent-impact.html#hawkes-flocking-model).
The `impact` function reads the observed event counts.

### Bid-ask price model

[Combine state-dependent baseline and component adjustments](state-dependent-impact.html#bid-ask-price-model).
The model uses marked price changes and the current `lambda_component_n` matrix.

## Point processes with flexible residuals

FRPP-specific functionality is planned to move to the separate
[frpp package](https://ksublee.github.io/frpp/). Use its
[FRPP examples](https://ksublee.github.io/frpp/articles/frpp-examples.html)
for `fspec()`, `fsim()` and `ffit()`. The full examples previously shown here,
including the original emhawkes fitting code, are preserved in the
[compatibility vignette](https://ksublee.github.io/frpp/articles/emhawkes-compatibility.html).

Simple custom-residual models can still use `set_residual()`, `hsim()` and
`logLik()` in emhawkes. These functions remain available during the transition;
this documentation change does not remove or deprecate them. For example:

```{r simple-flexible-residual, message=FALSE}
library(emhawkes)
h_residual <- set_residual(
  new("hspec", mu = 0.5, alpha = 1, beta = 1.2),
  param = c(a = 0.7, ell = 1.6),
  dresidual = dtzexp, presidual = ptzexp,
  qresidual = qtzexp, rresidual = rtzexp
)
set.seed(1107)
path_residual <- hsim(h_residual, size = 100, lambda_component0 = 0)
logLik(h_residual, inter_arrival = path_residual$inter_arrival,
       lambda_component0 = 0)
```

Hawkes goodness-of-fit residual diagnostics remain part of emhawkes; see
[Fitting and inference](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/fitting-and-inference.html#residual-process).
